output.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
output.body:
Scope creep is usually a sign that the workflow was never bounded clearly enough. Before you build, choose one recurring task, one success measure, and one point where new requests stop belonging to this pilot. If the work starts as “customer questions answered faster,” then the scope is the repeatable question-handling loop, not the whole inbox, the website, and the sales process in one go. That is where small projects get slippery.

A practical next step is to write a one-page scope note before any automation work begins. Keep it simple: what repeats, what counts as success, what is explicitly out of scope, and who approves any change. If a new request shows up later, the answer is not “yes, maybe later.” It is “that is a separate workflow.”

For a small business owner, this does two things. It makes the pilot testable, and it gives you a clean reason to defer adjacent ideas without arguing with the software. Bareni’s normal sequence is a free diagnostic, then a one-page proposal with scope, price, and measures, then a working MVP in a bounded slice of work. The timings are intended scopes, not guarantees, and final approval stays human. No heroics required.
